implementation_notes: Kotlin's own concurrency model replaces the classic structure rather than hand-writing it: hold idle instances in a plain ArrayDeque inside the pool class and bound outstanding leases with a kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore, whose acquire() suspends the caller instead of blocking a thread and whose withPermit { } releases the permit on every exit path; checkout becomes a suspend function returning a lease the caller closes with use { }. No factory hierarchy is needed - a lambda creates instances - and the free list only ever mutates inside one actor-style class. On the JVM you can equally delegate to Apache Commons Pool 2 or HikariCP through Java interop; keep the coroutine version when you need suspension-aware waiting without a thread per waiter.
pitfalls: Coroutines interleave at suspension points: never await while the free list is mid-update, and re-check shared state after every suspension rather than caching a decision made before it.
Semaphore.release() throws IllegalStateException when called more times than acquire() was - a double-close or a lost permit from a cancelled path breaks the bound permanently.
Blocking calls (JDBC, file I/O) inside use { } pin a carrier thread; run them on Dispatchers.IO, otherwise a small pool starves the whole dispatcher.
